structured_output.summary: External search for the open hypotheses. (1) A new FLOP-neutral time lever, also relevant to H4.5: torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark_limit exists in torch 2.4 (default 10 per the 1.13 docs; 0 = try every algorithm). It applies to cuDNN v8 convs, and since benchmarking happens in the untimed build, it is free to try. Energy-autotuning work suggests that time-optimal and energy-optimal kernels differ, which matters on a power-capped GPU. (2) H6.5.4: the EMA-dynamics paper (2411.18704) directly supports the BN-mismatch explanation. Parameters tolerate longer averaging windows than BN statistics do, recomputing BN statistics for the same EMA model recovers full performance, and it 'always improves generalization'. (3) A new structural time lever, late freezing of early layers (FreezeOut, Drop-Muon, Composer): it skips the full backward of group 1 in the energy-bound 32 px phase. Priors are mixed: ResNets ~20% speedup with no loss, VGG-like nets no gain, Composer CIFAR-100 ResNet-56 +0.4 pp at 5% speed from a single run, ImageNet a poor trade-off. Note that E093 already showed early-parameter freezing can hurt here. (4) A derived H10/H2.11 alternative: Muon's update norm is set by the lr, not the gradient, so the update-count gain may really be a path-length gain. A Muon lr bump in the 32 px phase only would test this at zero time cost. (5) InfoBatch removes E012's extra-forward failure mode (it prunes using losses already computed, with gradient rescaling and annealing), but it was validated only at 200 epochs, so the prior here is low. (6) Dead ends: 2:4 sparse training (torchao install not allowed, linear-only, 6% on ViT-L); no public CIFAR-100 speedrun submissions beyond futurebiohackers; no literature support for decreasing batch size late (the literature increases it); the critical-damping momentum schedule weakens on CIFAR-100. The hiverge/Fable recipes contain nothing untried that is cheap and allowed: frozen BN weight, SiLU, LS 0.09, TTA (banned) and mega CUDA graphs are each closed or disallowed by the tree's evidence.

findings.claim: torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark_limit exists in torch 2.4: 'the maximum number of cuDNN convolution algorithms to try when torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark is True. Set benchmark_limit to zero to try every available algorithm.' Older docs give a default of 10 and say it only affects convolutions dispatched through the cuDNN v8 API, which 'potentially exposes many more kernels'; the limit exists because trying all of them makes the first iteration slow.
findings.relevance: This is a new, untried, math-neutral time lever. Benchmarking happens in the untimed build, so setting benchmark_limit=0 costs nothing in score and may find faster conv fwd/dgrad/wgrad kernels for the 16/24/28/32 px static shapes (convs are 64-69% of GPU time, E067). It also bears on H4.5: a wider search may change which algorithm sets get picked and how often they differ between processes. Cheap test: build with limit=0 and log the per-phase epoch times and the cuDNN kernel names against the default.

findings.claim: GPU auto-tuning work with energy monitoring treats the kernel configuration that minimizes execution time and the one that maximizes energy efficiency as distinct objectives and studies how they differ (abstract only; no numbers retrieved).
findings.relevance: The 32/24 px phases sit at the 400 W cap (E045), and the judge is a 300 W PCIe card. cudnn.benchmark picks kernels by uncapped benchmark time in build, which may not be the fastest choice under sustained power capping. This weakly supports treating cuDNN algorithm selection (benchmark_limit, or pinning picks that win on throughput under the cap) as a time lever, not just a noise source.

findings.claim: 'Model parameters tolerate larger averaging window sizes than BN statistics.' With slow EMA decay the EMA model degrades or diverges, but 'if we recompute the BN stats of that same EMA model ... we recover full performance, indicating that it is BN that breaks an EMA model as we increase the size of the averaging window.' Also: 'recomputing BN stats always improves generalization'; with recomputed statistics, longer windows help.
findings.relevance: This is direct external support for mechanism (b) in H6.5: the averaged weights mismatch the BN buffers copied from the net, and the mismatch grows with window length. That fits E081 (20-step window, -0.09) and E083 (uniform LAWA, -0.29). It raises the prior for H6.5.4 (average the BN buffers over the same snapshots, as with AveragedModel(use_buffers=True)). Caution: E018's cumulative BN re-estimation on the SGD/E006 base lost 0.34 pp, so averaging the buffers is the safer version and costs no extra forward pass.

findings.claim: FreezeOut (freezing early layers progressively and dropping them from the backward pass) on CIFAR: up to 20% wall-clock saving with no accuracy loss for ResNets, up to 3% relative error increase for DenseNets, and no improvement for VGG. Composer layer freezing: CIFAR-100 ResNet-56 ~5% faster with accuracy 75.82 -> 76.22 (no replicates); ResNet-50 ImageNet ~5% faster at -0.5 to -1 pp, 'not an especially good speed vs accuracy tradeoff'; freeze_start should be >=0.1.
findings.relevance: This is a new FLOP/energy lever for the energy-bound 32 px phase, which is ~71% of time and binding for epoch trims. Freezing group 1 (and the stem) for the last ~1-1.5 epochs, when the LR is near the 0.05 floor, skips group 1's entire backward (wgrad + dgrad, ~2/3 of its ~20% conv share). My rough estimate is a 2-4% total-time saving. Priors are mixed: the VGG-like case, closest to this net, showed no gain, and E093 shows that early-parameter freezes can cost a lot here. It needs one extra static graph variant, warmed up in build.

findings.claim: Drop-Muon updates only the layers from a sampled index to the output on each step, truncating backprop at the first active layer, so the frozen layers' backward and optimizer work are skipped. On 3-layer CNNs (MNIST/F-MNIST/CIFAR-10, bs 8192-32768, constant lr 0.1) it is up to 1.4x faster in wall clock than full Muon at comparable final accuracy. The CIFAR-10 gains are smaller. The authors note that Drop-Muon could take larger step sizes.
findings.relevance: This is a Muon-specific variant of the late-freeze lever. On CIFAR-10 the gains are small, and the setting (huge batches, constant lr, no BN-heavy speedrun net) is far from the tip, so it is weak evidence. A random per-step skip would also break static-graph efficiency, so a deterministic late freeze of group 1 is the practical form.

findings.claim: Muon replaces each 2D update with an (approximately) orthogonalized version, so its update scale is set by the learning rate (and the shape scaling), not by the gradient magnitude.
findings.relevance: Derived hypothesis for H10/H2.11.4: with fixed-size Muon steps, bs 1024 at 32 px (E084/E095) increases the total path length of the 32 px filters by ~1.4x as well as the update count. A Muon lr raised only in the 32 px phase (e.g. 0.24 -> 0.28-0.30 there, as a 0-d tensor, at bs 1536) would separate 'more updates' from 'more movement' at zero time cost. If it recovers the ~+0.11 pp off-seed gain, it funds a cut without the +2.5% time. This differs from H7.1.3, which raises the lr globally including the low-res phases. E034 (lr 0.20 flat) was measured on an older, global, bs-1024 base.

findings.claim: InfoBatch: each epoch, randomly prune a fraction r=0.5 of the samples whose loss is below the mean, using losses recorded in the previous epoch (no extra forward pass), and rescale the remaining low-loss samples' gradients by 1/(1-r). Prune only in the first 87.5% of epochs (annealing). CIFAR-100 ResNet-50, 200 epochs: 80.6±0.1 full vs 80.6±0.2 InfoBatch at ~34% cost saved. At equal compute, full-data training got 79.4 vs 80.6.
findings.relevance: It fixes E012's failure mode (the extra scoring forward cost nearly what it saved), because the losses come from the sample's previous training forward. It is validated only at 200 epochs, though. At ~7 epochs few samples are 'learned', and at fixed batch size pruning removes steps, which H10 says costs ~0.1 pp per 25% of steps. Low prior; at most, prune only in 32 px epochs 2-3 at r~0.3.

findings.claim: 2:4 semi-structured sparse training (torchao SemiSparseLinear) gives 1.3x on the ViT-L MLP linear layers and 6% end-to-end on A100, with sparsity for 70% of training followed by dense.
findings.relevance: Negative for this task. It needs torchao (installs are forbidden), covers only nn.Linear (the cost here is in convs), and the end-to-end gain is small. Do not pursue.

findings.claim: The public CIFAR-100 speedrun repo has no pull requests and one fresh fork, so there are no public submissions beyond futurebiohackers (airbench96-style SGD, 75.29% in 8.11 s on Modal A100-SXM4; Muon 'lost to SGD at every size' in their sweep). The fetched README says official judging is 40 trials on an A100 80GB PCIe, while a search snippet of the README says L40S 48GB and 50 trials, so the repo has had more than one version.
findings.relevance: No external CIFAR-100 recipe beyond the tip's lineage exists to mine; the tip (Muon) is already well past the public state of the art. The judge-hardware discrepancy is only a provenance note (task.md governs). If the judge were ever an L40S, energy/FLOP levers would transfer better than per-step levers, as H2.4 already assumes for the 300 W PCIe card.

findings.claim: hiverge: SiLU, BN momentum 0.5566 with eps 1e-12 and frozen affine weight, Muon lr 0.205 / momentum 0.655 / wd 1.04e-6*bs, SGD momentum 0.825, LS 0.09, bs 1536, no warmup, no lookahead, whitening bias trained for 0.2 epoch, TTA on the 25% least-confident samples. Fable e1: Muon lr 0.2255, 8.875 epochs with decay over 8.5 and a 0.05 floor, res schedule 3@24/3@28/3@32, final EMA 0.7 every 4 steps starting 8 steps before decay end, plus per-step and whole-run 'mega' CUDA graphs.
findings.relevance: Cross-check for unexplored differences: none remain that are both cheap and allowed. TTA is banned. SiLU (E003), LS (E009/E037), the bias freeze (E061/E093), lookahead removal (E092) and CUDA graphs (E052, GPU 98-100% busy) are all closed by the tree's own evidence. Fable's resolution schedule gives 1/3 of epochs to 28 px, which supports continuing H2.17 (28 px substitution keeps the step count), but its gain was measured on CIFAR-10 only.

findings.claim: The adaptive-batch literature (AdaBatch; 'Don't decay the LR, increase the batch size') increases the batch late in training, which is equivalent to decaying the LR. I found no work reporting that a smaller batch late in training improves final accuracy.
findings.relevance: E084/E095 (smaller batch in the late 32 px phase helps) run against the SGD-era literature. That fits the Muon-specific path-length explanation (finding 6) better than a generic noise or generalization one. It weakly favors testing a 32 px-only Muon lr increase before spending more time on per-phase batch sizes.

findings.claim: A critical-damping momentum schedule μ(t)=1-2√α(t) reached 90% on CIFAR-10 2.34x faster than μ=0.9 but lost 0.46 pp in final accuracy; a hybrid recovered it. The gain weakened on CIFAR-100 (1.14x when accuracy-matched). This was on ResNet-18 with 200-epoch SGD.
findings.relevance: Low-prior scalar knob. Muon momentum is already flat in 0.5-0.6 (E030) and steep above it (E027). The CIFAR-100 weakening and the SGD/long-schedule setting make it unlikely to pay here. Do not prioritize.
